The Giver, Lois Lowry's dystopian novel that won the Newbery Medal in 1994. Jonas lives in a seemingly perfect, colorless society where all pain, choice, and emotion have been eliminated through conformity and medication. In this world, precision language eliminates ambiguity, color has been engineered out of human perception entirely, and citizens are assigned their life roles at a ceremonial age. When Jonas is chosen to become the Receiver of Memory, he begins training with an elderly man called the Giver, who transfers all of human history—joy, suffering, beauty, and pain—directly into Jonas's mind. Jonas discovers that the Giver carries the emotional and historical weight of the entire civilization alone. The Giver has seen color, felt love, experienced music—all invisible to everyone else. As Jonas learns more, he realizes that his friend Fiona is scheduled for "release," which means death, along with his father, a Nurturer, as part of the society's management of population. The society maintains order through enforced sameness, and the cost of such order is the elimination of genuine choice. The ending is deliberately ambiguous. Jonas escapes with a baby and finds either freedom or death, suggesting that choice and risk are inseparable from meaning and humanity. The novel became one of the most widely taught children's books, sparking debate about how freedom and individual difference are the price of true life.
